# US DOE, Human Performance Improvement Handbook Vol. 2: Human Performance Tools (light reference)

**Source:** U.S. Department of Energy (2009). *Human Performance Improvement Handbook, Volume 2: Human Performance Tools for Individuals, Work Teams, and Management*. DOE-HDBK-1028-2009, June 2009. Distribution Statement A, public release. Public domain (US Government work, 17 USC §105); DOE asks for acknowledgement in reuse. Third-party material inside it is paraphrased, never quoted: Sections 1 and 2 (the Foreword says their tools come primarily from two INPO good-practice guides), the three survey instruments (adapted from INPO and the Naval Postgraduate School), and the just-culture, culpability and investigation material that Volume 1 credits to Reason, Johnston and Dekker.
**Structure:** Foreword; Introduction with a when-to-use matrix; Section 1, tools for individuals (12 tools); Section 2, tools for work teams (13 tools, four of them checking and verification practices); Section 3, management tools for finding latent weaknesses (11 tools, the Culpability Decision Tree and three survey instruments); Definitions. Every tool is set out as Overview, Use the Tool, Recommended Practices, At-Risk Practices. 137 pages, read in full; text-only image scope.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

Volume 2 is the practical companion to Volume 1: "a set of practical methods and techniques for anticipating, preventing, and catching active human errors; and, more importantly, identifying and mitigating latent errors attributable to organizational factors" [V] (Foreword, p. i). It restates Volume 1's paradigm of reducing error and managing controls to reach zero significant events. "This handbook is not a requirements document" [V]; it is a menu from which organisations choose, and they should not change tools that already work (Foreword, p. ii).

The tools are no substitute for competence or thought: workers first need a solid grounding in the technical fundamentals of their equipment and processes, and "Safety is not obtained by mindlessly applying human performance tools" [V] (Introduction, p. 1). The work splits three ways: tools one person can use on any task (Section 1), tools that need two or more people and supervisory support (Section 2), both aimed at active errors at the point of work, and tools for managers to find the latent organisational weaknesses that provoke error and weaken defences (Section 3) (Introduction, p. 1; Sec 3, p. 70).

## Tools for individuals (Sec 1)

The individual tools help a performer keep positive control, so that what is intended to happen is what happens and nothing else; they deliberately slow work down to avoid the delays that follow events, and aim at critical steps (Sec 1, p. 5). Many are situational-awareness tools, said to be particularly helpful in skill-mode work, with Procedure Use and Adherence and Validate Assumptions singled out for rule-based work (Sec 1, p. 5).

- **Task Preview** with S-A-F-E-R: summarise critical steps, anticipate errors and precursors, foresee consequences, evaluate controls and contingencies, review experience (Sec 1, pp. 6–7).
- **Job-Site Review**: a few minutes walking the area for hazards, trip-sensitive equipment, the right component, critical indicators and error precursors, building healthy uneasiness (Sec 1, pp. 8–9).
- **Questioning Attitude**: in the field, stop–look–listen, ask, proceed only if sure, otherwise stop, with "danger words" such as "I assume" as cues; in planning, F-A-C-T-S, guarding against "cookbooking" and rules of thumb that lead to rule-based errors (Sec 1, pp. 10–15).
- **Pause When Unsure**: in the knowledge-based mode, with a 10–50 percent error chance, stop, make safe, notify the supervisor and get help; it supplements formal Stop Work processes (Sec 1, pp. 16–17).
- **Self-Checking** with STAR (Stop, Think, Act, Review): particularly effective for skill-based, repetitive work, with attention peaking when a component's status changes (Sec 1, pp. 18–19).
- **Procedure Use and Adherence**: follow as written and in sequence, but stop when a step cannot be done safely as written, because procedures can hide flaws (Sec 1, pp. 20–21).
- **Validate Assumptions**: document, evidence, walk down, and close out every unverified assumption before delivery (Sec 1, pp. 22–23).
- **Signature**: before signing, affirm knowledge, involvement, independence, quality, right and proper, and no doubt (Sec 1, pp. 24–25).
- **Effective Communication**: three-way (repeat-back) communication and the phonetic alphabet, effective communication being called probably the most important defence against errors and events (Sec 1, pp. 26–28).
- **Place-Keeping** against omitted or repeated steps, and the **Do Not Disturb sign** to protect knowledge workers doing critical reviews (Sec 1, pp. 29–31).

## Tools for work teams (Sec 2)

- **Pre-Job Briefing**, graded by hazard and complexity into four kinds; most events occur during so-called routine activities, and the detailed agenda covers critical-step tools, operating experience, stop-work criteria and performers' concerns (Sec 2, pp. 34–37). The **Technical Task Pre-Job Briefing** adapts it to office work, with "reverse" briefings where the performer leads (Sec 2, pp. 38–40).
- **Checking and verification**: checking confirms a correct action; verification confirms equipment condition or document accuracy. Peer-checking (the least rigorous) prevents the performer's wrong act; concurrent verification confirms condition side by side, without true independence; independent verification, separated in time and distance, tends to catch more errors; peer review checks another's work product in three readings (Sec 2, pp. 41–50).
- **Flagging** against returning to a similar but wrong component; **Turnover** to give the on-coming person an accurate mental model (Sec 2, pp. 51–53).
- **Post-Job Reviews** (field and technical) collect pluses and deltas so management can remove latent weaknesses before they accumulate; the technical version states that errors causing significant events are organisational failures (Sec 2, pp. 54–57).
- **Project Planning**, **Problem Solving with PACTS** (a knowledge-based situation, error chance 1:2 to 1:10), **Decision Making** (forward-looking and conservative, putting safety ahead of near-term production, with a devil's advocate), **Project Review Meetings** and **Vendor Oversight** (VENDOR) (Sec 2, pp. 58–69).

## Management tools (Sec 3)

Latent weaknesses are undetected deficiencies in organisational processes or values that create error-provoking conditions or degrade defences; "Once they are created they do not fade away but rather accumulate in the system" [V], so managers should find and correct them early (Sec 3, p. 70).

- **Benchmarking** overcomes "paradigm blindness"; visits without follow-through are "industrial tourism" (Sec 3, pp. 71–72).
- **Observations** look at the whole job, not just behaviour; "The purpose is not to criticize or to judge people" [V], and managers in the field reduce error rates (Sec 3, pp. 73–74).
- **Self-Assessments** can be the most effective way to find latent weaknesses, provided work is not staged for the assessor (Sec 3, pp. 75–76).
- **Performance Indicators**: lagging (results) and leading (system health); things are often counted because they can be; seven selection criteria; two or three indicators per objective; statistical analysis rather than knee-jerk reaction to sparse data (Sec 3, pp. 77–79).
- **Independent Oversight** is reverse benchmarking; outsiders spot weaknesses insiders miss, and defensiveness wastes the chance (Sec 3, pp. 80–82).
- **Work Product Review** grades knowledge workers' products A to D and feeds back face to face (Sec 3, pp. 83–84).
- **Operating Experience** rests on the claim that serious accidents are almost always preceded by less serious precursor events; it combats "It can't happen here" (Sec 3, pp. 90–92).
- **Change Management**: everyday changes to crews, schedules, procedures and equipment are changes too, and unstructured change raises managers' own error potential; an eleven-step process (Sec 3, pp. 93–94).

## Investigating events and reporting errors

The investigation tool sets a traditional view, which blames individual competence, attention or attitude, against a view of human error as a symptom of deeper trouble in the system and the start rather than the end of an investigation, aimed at preventing recurrence rather than punishment (Sec 3, p. 85). It warns against hindsight, recommends debriefing participants before learning the event's details, and reconstructs at each critical juncture what people saw, knew, expected and aimed at, explaining why their actions made sense at the time; it then works through Volume 1's Anatomy of an Event to failed defences, precursors and organisational contributors (Sec 3, pp. 85–89).

Most organisations do not gather feedback on human errors well, and a culture change may be needed first (Sec 3, p. 95). A just culture is the required prerequisite: no tolerance for recklessness, honest errors unpunished, people judged by intent rather than consequence, with foresight, culpability and substitution tests and a Culpability Decision Tree running from individual to organisational culpability (Sec 3, pp. 96–99). Reporting barriers (embarrassment, fear of the record, scepticism, effort) are met by de-identification, protection and separation of functions, rapid feedback and easy reporting (Sec 3, p. 97).

## Surveys

Three instruments, all adapted from outside sources and paraphrased: a safety climate survey of employee attitudes, a leadership-team gap analysis rating seven attribute groups from strength to problem, and a job-site conditions questionnaire organised by direction, opportunity and willingness to act (Sec 3, pp. 101–127).

## How the tools map to error types

Skill-based slips and lapses: self-checking, place-keeping, flagging, the Do Not Disturb sign and communication tools. Rule-based: procedure use and adherence, validate assumptions, the planning-stage questioning attitude, decision making. Knowledge-based: pause when unsure, PACTS, decision making. Peer-checking targets wrong actions; concurrent and independent verification target wrong conditions; peer review targets defects in work products. Sections 1 and 2 address active errors; Section 3 addresses latent weaknesses (Sec 1, pp. 5, 13, 16, 18; Sec 2, pp. 41–46, 61, 63; Sec 3, p. 70).

## Key Statistics

- Error chance when unsure (knowledge-based): 10–50 percent (Sec 1, p. 16); in problem solving, 1:2 to 1:10 (Sec 2, p. 61).
- Indicators: seven criteria rated 1–5; two or three per objective (Sec 3, pp. 78–79).
- Peer review: three readings (Sec 2, p. 50). Work product grades: four (Sec 3, p. 84). Change management: eleven steps (Sec 3, pp. 93–94).

## Key Connections

- INPO: primary source of the individual and work-team tools; source of two survey instruments.
- Naval Postgraduate School: source of the safety climate survey.
- DOE HPI Handbook Volume 1: the companion volume, cited for the culpability methods and the Anatomy of an Event.
- NNSA activity-level work planning guidance; DOE oversight and OE directives.

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Tools applied mindlessly, or procedures "cookbooked", do not produce safety.
2. "Routine" does not mean "no risk"; most events occur during so-called routine work.
3. Following a procedure without question does not guarantee safety.
4. Investigations should not hunt for people to punish with hindsight; error is the starting point.
5. People should not be judged by the consequences of honest errors.
6. Counting what is easy to count is not performance measurement.
